questions.q: What is the real throughline connecting all ten chapters of this course, per the wrap-up?
options: Querying fundamentals are remarkably portable across platforms; procedural code is where the real divergence lives
Every SQL dialect is completely different with no portable concepts at all
Only Oracle and PostgreSQL share any real similarities
Procedural code is portable; querying syntax is where divergence lives
questions.explain: The capstone and Chapter 4 both showed querying syntax (SELECT/JOIN/GROUP BY/window functions) stays nearly identical across platforms, while Chapters 5-8 showed procedural code is where real, structural divergence happens.

questions.q: What did the Lesson 60 capstone prove about the join graph, GROUP BY, CTE, and window function in the reporting query?
options: They worked structurally unchanged across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL
They required a complete rewrite on every single platform
Only T-SQL could execute that query structure at all
GROUP BY was the only piece that transferred across platforms
questions.explain: The capstone's four translations kept the same querying structure throughout -- only small, specific syntax differences like the concatenation operator needed changes.

questions.q: Why does T-SQL fluency NOT automatically transfer to a new platform's procedural idioms, according to this lesson?
options: Procedural features like TRY/CATCH, packages, and cursors behave differently enough across platforms that each one needs to be deliberately learned on its own terms
T-SQL and every other platform's procedural code are identical, so no new learning is ever needed
Procedural code doesn't exist on any platform other than T-SQL
Querying fundamentals are the only part of SQL that ever differs between platforms
questions.explain: Chapters 5-8 showed real structural differences -- TRY/CATCH has no MySQL equivalent, Oracle packages don't exist in T-SQL -- so procedural idioms need deliberate platform-specific learning, not an assumption of transfer.

questions.q: What practical habit does this lesson recommend carrying forward after the course ends?
options: Keeping a personal, growing dialect cheat sheet built from real differences encountered on the job
Memorizing every function name on every platform before writing any code
Avoiding documentation entirely and relying only on this course's content
Rewriting every stored procedure from scratch on every new platform without checking references
questions.explain: The lesson recommends starting a personal cheat sheet, noting real differences as they come up at work -- the same process that produced Lesson 59's own five-item checklist.

questions.q: How should a developer treat a new platform's procedural layer, per this lesson's closing advice?
options: As its own thing to learn on purpose, not as 'T-SQL with different keywords'
As identical to T-SQL in every meaningful way
As unnecessary to learn, since migration tools handle it automatically
As something that only matters for DBAs, never developers
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns against assuming T-SQL knowledge transfers directly to procedural code on a new platform -- each platform's idioms need deliberate attention.
